name: Stone
flavor: Grey. Heavy. Karl's best friend and most frequent conversation partner.

name: Stick
flavor: A stick of exceptional quality. So says Karl, and he has seen many sticks.

name: Dry grass
flavor: Bone-dry and highly flammable. For now, Karl uses it as a pillow.

name: Water
flavor: Wet. Karl has tasted it and can confirm: very wet.

name: Clay
flavor: Soft and mouldable. Much like Karl's relationship with good ideas.

name: Berries
flavor: Possibly edible. Karl uses the bird test: if the bird survives, it's lunch.

name: Grubs
flavor: They wriggle. Karl watches them a little too long and a little too fondly.

name: Wild boar
flavor: A boar that has observed Karl for three days and remains unimpressed.

name: Sparks
flavor: Tiny stars that live for half a second. Karl applauds every time.
note: Stone Age fire-starting struck flint against pyrite — two ordinary stones really can make sparks.

name: Fire
flavor: Warm, glowing, and not at all fond of being touched. Karl discovered that part personally.
note: Humans have controlled fire for at least 400,000 years — traces from Wonderwerk Cave suggest up to a million.

name: Stone axe
flavor: A rock on a stick. Humanity's first subscription to tools.
note: The oldest stone tools are over 2.5 million years old — older than modern humans themselves.

name: Spear
flavor: Pointy at one end. Karl held the wrong one first.
note: The Schöningen spears from Germany are about 300,000 years old — the world's oldest preserved hunting weapons.

name: Meat
flavor: Fresh from a boar that underestimated Karl. A mistake nobody saw coming.
note: Eating meat accelerated human brain evolution — more energy per bite than any plant.

name: Roast meat
flavor: Crispy outside, juicy inside. Karl has invented gastronomy and is never going back.
note: Cooked food gave humans more calories for less chewing — a possible key to our big brains.

name: Roasted grubs
flavor: Crispy. Nutty. Karl says 'mmm'. The narrator says nothing, very loudly.
note: Around two billion people eat insects today — grubs are rich in protein and climate-friendly.

name: Mud
flavor: Clay plus water. Karl calls it 'soft dirt' and is very proud of the name.
note: Mud and clay were humanity's first building materials — sun-dried bricks are over 9,000 years old.

name: Mud bath
flavor: Karl rolls thoroughly. He calls it skincare. The boar nods in approval.
note: Pigs really do use mud baths as sunscreen and insect protection — early humans possibly did too.

name: Pottery
flavor: Baked clay that holds water. Karl's first pot is crooked, and he loves it.
note: The world's oldest pottery is about 20,000 years old, found in Xianrendong Cave in China.

name: Steam
flavor: The water hisses and vanishes into the air. Karl is deeply offended on the water's behalf.
note: Steam power was demonstrated in antiquity with Heron's aeolipile — but only changed the world in the 1700s.

name: Ore
flavor: Glittering stones from the rock face. Karl thinks it's decoration. It's the future.
note: The oldest known mines are over 40,000 years old — long before anyone knew what metal was.

name: Copper
flavor: Shiny, reddish, and bendable. Karl has tried biting it. Twice.
note: Humans have worked copper for almost 10,000 years — the oldest finds come from Anatolia.

name: Bronze
flavor: Harder than copper, fancier than stone. Karl made a lump and shows it to everyone.
note: Bronze — copper alloyed with tin — emerged around 3300 BC and gave its name to an entire era.

name: Grub farm
flavor: A clay bowl of well-groomed grubs. Karl has named them all. Every one is called Bent.
note: Insect farming is a growing industry today — grubs turn food waste into protein better than any livestock.

name: Wild grain
flavor: Tiny seeds on stalks. A woman from the next valley claims you can eat them. Karl is skeptical.

name: Ox
flavor: Big, strong, and surprisingly willing to cooperate. More than can be said for Karl.
